27 November 2026 · Fire TV Cube 3 with Tesseract VP · measured with a 10-bit HDMI capture card

What the Cube's HDMI output carries

We captured the Cube's HDMI output and a PC's HDMI output with a capture card and compared every captured frame with the values it should hold. All results are from one Cube, one capture card and one PC, on this chain. Counts are given next to each result.

In plain wordsAnswerThe questions askedRig and methodTest materialPath A: PC directPath B: Cube playbackPath C: Cube HDMI inputChroma and detailFound and fixedConclusionsLimits

In plain words

Does the Cube change the picture on its way to your TV or projector?

  • Films the Cube plays itself: no, when it sends 10 or 12-bit. We checked every shade in a test picture and every one arrived exactly as it left the file.
  • At 8-bit it adds very fine noise (called dither) to fake the in-between shades. You would not see it at normal viewing, but it is not an exact copy.
  • Tone mapping changes the picture on purpose, to fit HDR into what your display can show. That is the job it is meant to do.
  • Colours depend on one setting, Colour space. Pick the one that matches how your display is set up (BT.709 for most TVs, BT.2020 for a wide-colour projector set to BT.2020, or Auto). Each setting sends exactly what it says.
  • Things plugged into the Cube's HDMI input (a games console, a PC) come through very close to the original, but not exact: the Cube changes them by a tiny amount and adds fine noise for some input settings.
  • Two bugs were found and fixed: colours on RGB output were slightly wrong (fixed in the 27 November Nightly), and Match the film did not switch the refresh rate with one Kodi build (fix not released yet).
A few terms used on this page
  • Code: the number that stores one shade. A 10-bit picture has 1024 of them per colour; "1 code off" is the smallest possible difference.
  • Bit-exact: every number in the picture arrives unchanged.
  • 10-bit, 12-bit, 8-bit: how many shades the HDMI signal can carry. More bits, finer steps.
  • RGB, 4:4:4, 4:2:2: ways of packing colour into the HDMI signal. 4:2:2 stores colour at half the width of the detail; 4:4:4 and RGB store it in full.
  • Passthrough: HDR sent to the display untouched, for displays that do their own tone mapping.
  • Dither: fine noise that lets fewer bits imitate more shades.
  • Capture card: a PC card that records exactly what arrives on an HDMI cable, so we can compare it with the file.

The answer

Bit-exact for decoded video at 10 and 12-bit; 8-bit is dithered; the HDMI input is close but not exact

For video the Cube decodes itself, played with HDR passthrough and sent at 10 or 12-bit, the captured ramp held all 877 codes (64 to 940) unchanged in every format and refresh rate the card could lock, in our tests. Flat fields, gradients and added noise also came through code for code. At 8-bit the transmitter dithers, without bias. RGB output needed a colour-matrix fix, which is in the 27 November Nightly. Colour on SDR pictures depends on the Colour space setting: BT.709 and Auto send the plain decode, BT.2020 re-expresses SDR colour for a wide-gamut display. A PC picture fed through the Cube's HDMI input arrived within 1 to 2 codes of 1023 at best, and was not bit-exact in any of the four input formats we tried; the same picture sent straight from the PC to the card was exact.

In practice: 10 and 12-bit, 4:2:2, 4:4:4 and RGB from the Cube

  • Exact in our tests: films the Cube plays itself, HDR passthrough, at 10 or 12-bit in YCbCr 4:2:2, YCbCr 4:4:4 or RGB, at 23.976 to 60 Hz.
  • What the card could not prove: the lowest 2 bits of a 12-bit signal (it records 10), and full 4:4:4 colour resolution (it converts YCbCr to 4:2:2 on the way in). 4:4:4 colour patches came out exact, but fine colour detail at 4:4:4 is unverified.
  • On the current Stable release: RGB output uses the wrong colour matrix (fixed in the 27 November Nightly; YCbCr was never affected). With Match the film the chosen format may not apply at the film's rate, and with the stock Kodi 22.0-ALPHA1 build the rate does not switch; that fix is not released yet.
  • Not bit-exact by design or by limit: 8-bit output (dithered, unbiased), SDR out and HDR10 out (tone mapped on purpose), and sources on the HDMI input (within 1 to 2 codes at best, and dithered when the input is limited range).
  • Unexplained once: one 1080p59.94 run carried 8-bit data while reporting 10 and 12-bit; it did not repeat in two later runs.

What this means for viewers. Video the Cube decodes, sent at 10 or 12-bit, arrived unchanged in our tests, so choose 10 or 12-bit output where the display accepts it. 8-bit output is dithered. A source on the HDMI input picks up a small conversion error, about 1 to 2 codes of 1023.

The questions asked

Four questions were raised about the Cube's output. Each answer below says what we measured, with the count, and links to the detail.

1. Does a 10-bit HDR10 greyscale ramp survive at the HDMI output?

Yes, at 10 and 12-bit output. A ramp holding every code from 64 to 940 came out with all 877 codes and error 0, in RGB, YCbCr 4:4:4 and 4:2:2, at 23.976 to 60 Hz (65 of 66 format and rate settings; the one exception is unexplained). At 8-bit output the same ramp has 220 levels, dithered without bias. Path B

2. How does HDR passthrough compare with tone mapping to the display's peak?

Passthrough sends the source unchanged; tone mapping changes it on purpose. In passthrough the ramp was exact. With tone mapping (SDR out, or HDR10 out at a lower peak) the values are reshaped to fit the display, so they are not compared code for code. At 10-bit the tone-mapped output stayed neutral (R=G=B), had no added noise and no dither; the ramp's 877 codes became 616 levels (SDR out) and 460 (HDR10 out at a 120-nit target), rising throughout except for 1 to 2-code steps back in the highlight roll-off. Tone-mapped output

3. Does Fire OS dither HDR10 to 8-bit 4:4:4 whatever the output mode?

Not on this Cube with Tesseract VP installed. Dither appeared only when the output itself was 8-bit. At 10 and 12-bit (RGB, 4:4:4, 4:2:2) flat fields had no spatial or temporal noise and the ramp was exact, in passthrough, SDR out and HDR10 out. Two cautions: we did not measure a Cube without Tesseract VP, so the report about stock Fire OS is neither confirmed nor refuted; and when the output format is left to Fire OS it can land on 8-bit RGB (it did at film rates on the released build), which is then dithered. Path B

4. Does the HDMI input path do the same?

The input path is not bit-exact, and it dithers when the input is limited range. A PC test image through the Cube's HDMI input came out within 1 code on greys at best (10-bit YCbCr 4:4:4 input), against 100% exact when the same PC fed the capture card directly. With limited-range input, 39 to 50% of samples changed from one frame to the next (by up to 3 codes with 10-bit input, up to 12 to 13 with 8-bit), the signature of a dither in the input's conversion; with full-range RGB input the frames were identical. Path C

Rig and method

Path A
PC → capture card

Checks the capture card and the method. A picture whose values are known goes straight in.

Path B
Cube plays a clip → capture card

What the Cube sends when it decodes the video itself (a player app on the Cube).

Path C
PC → Cube HDMI input → capture card

What the Cube does to an HDMI source passing through it. Compare with path A.

  • Reference. Path B clips were built from known code values (ramps, flat fields, patterns), or from a photo whose source Y'CbCr is known; the capture is compared with those values or with a BT.709 decode of the same source. Paths A and C show one 8-bit test image 1:1, full screen, with display scaling off.
  • What the card can prove. It records 10 bits per channel (RGB as r210, YCbCr as 4:2:2 v210), so a 12-bit signal is checked at its top 10 bits and YCbCr chroma is checked after the card's own 4:2:2 step. It locks up to 2160p30 and 1080p60. It has no HDCP, so HDCP was switched off on the Cube for each capture (a link flag, not the picture).
  • Settling. After every mode change the first 0 to 9 frames can still carry the previous colour matrix (see path B). All analysis captures were taken at least 3 s after the picture returned; any capture we dropped is noted with the reason.
  • Metrics. Distinct levels, exact columns or samples, max and mean error, R=G=B on greys, PSNR (10-bit peak 1023, and 8-bit peak 255 where noted), SSIM, MSE per channel, spatial and temporal standard deviation of flat fields, dEITP for colours, modulation for detail patterns.

8-bit output and its dither

At 8-bit the transmitter dithers. The pattern is spatially uncorrelated and cycles over 4 frames: a pixel carries the upper level in 1, 2 or 3 of every 4 frames when the fraction is 25, 50 or 75%. R, G and B share one mask, so grey stays grey. At 10 and 12-bit every flat field has spatial and temporal sd 0.00.

Tone-mapped output

SDR out and HDR10 out change the picture on purpose, to fit HDR into the display's range, so they are not compared code for code. What matters for the signal: at 10-bit, greys stay grey (R=G=B), flat fields have no noise (sd 0) and there is no dither; at 8-bit the same dither as in passthrough is added.

Colour on real pictures depends on the Colour space setting

Three photos as SDR BT.709 clips, RGB 10-bit output, colour fix active. Each capture was compared with two possible right answers: the plain BT.709 picture, and the same picture converted to BT.2020. How to read it: the capture matches the answer with the small number. The number is the typical difference in codes out of 1023 (RMS over R, G and B); 2 to 6 codes is the test clip's own compression, not the Cube.

PhotoColour spaceMatchesFrom the plain pictureFrom the BT.2020 versionCaptures
Street sceneAutoplain picture5.6274
Street sceneBT.709plain picture5.6273 of 5*
Street sceneBT.2020BT.2020 version264.93
Film frame, interiorAutoplain picture2.9101
Film frame, interiorBT.2020BT.2020 version113.41
Film frame, wideAutoplain picture3.0131
Film frame, wideBT.2020BT.2020 version142.91

Every setting matched the picture it is meant to send, in all 7 cases.

This is configuration, not an error. As the setting's own description says, BT.2020 (for a projector set to BT.2020) converts menus and SDR video into BT.2020 so they don't look oversaturated, and the display has to be in its wide-gamut mode. Auto flags each signal as what it is and converts nothing; BT.709 is for BT.709 displays. With BT.2020 the HDMI label for SDR stays BT.709; whether it should also say BT.2020 is an open design choice. Setting the label by hand changed only the label and the transmitter's matrix choice, not the captured RGB codes (5.1 codes from the BT.2020 version, against 4.9 without the label).

*Two first captures of a run were 24 codes off and did not reproduce in 3 repeats; they are listed, not used. With Tesseract VP switched off (the driver's own matrix), the street scene was 8.7 codes from the plain picture, against 5.6 with Auto and the colour fix.

What we found wrong, and fixed

RGB output used the BT.601 matrix

Greys were exact, colours were not: RGB output equalled YCbCr converted with BT.601, in passthrough, SDR out and HDR10 out. YCbCr 4:4:4 output was exact on all 18 patches. This error was there all the time on RGB output, not only after a mode change. The fix selects the matrix that matches the picture. With the fix, a much smaller left-over remains for up to 0.4 s after a mode change (see Settling). Status: in the Nightly of 27 November 2026; Stable still has the old behaviour until it is promoted.

Who it affected: only RGB output, 8-bit and 10/12-bit alike. That is any Cube with Colour format set to RGB, and the case where the output format is left to Fire OS and it picks RGB (in our tests the released build landed on RGB 8-bit at film rates). YCbCr output (4:4:4, 4:2:2, 4:2:0) was not affected.

Per-patch chart

Match the film with the stock Kodi build

It depends on the Kodi build. With stock Kodi 22.0-ALPHA1 the video layer reports no frame size, so the rate reading came back empty and the output stayed at 2160p59.94. With Kodi FEL 22.0-RC2 the frame size is reported and the match works. If you use another Kodi build, check that the output switches to the film's rate. A fix falls back to the decoder's own frame rate for Kodi, and re-applies the chosen colour format at the film's rate. Status: on a test branch, not released.

Limits

  • One of each. One Cube, one capture card, one PC. Where a row says one capture, it is one.
  • Not tested: protected streaming apps, game mode, Dolby Vision and HLG on the colour tests, HDR on the settling test, a 10-bit source on paths A and C (the PC desktop is 8-bit), 4K at 50 and 60 Hz (beyond the card), 12-bit least significant bits (the card records 10).
  • Older captures. A comparison with earlier 8-bit captures of other processors and a PC player is not in this page yet.
  • Unexplained, not reproduced: one 1080p59.94 block read as 8-bit data; two first captures of a run with higher error on one colour setting.
  • Moving pictures. Patterns and photos were static; per-frame behaviour of moving video, dropped or repeated frames and judder were not measured.
  • Stock Fire OS. No unmodified Cube was measured; everything here is Fire OS with Tesseract VP installed. Path C ran with Tesseract VP, which runs the HDMI input.
Measured 27 November 2026 on one Cube, one capture card and one PC.
